svg.title: The serving word
svg.desc: One Greek verb, diakoneō, to serve, joins three groups of texts. At the centre, Jesus: 'the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve' (Mark 10:45) and 'I am among you as the one who serves' (Luke 22:27). On the left, the women of Galilee: they 'provided for them out of their means' (Luke 8:3) and 'followed him and ministered to him' (Mark 15:41), both the same verb. On the right, Phoebe, 'a servant of the church at Cenchreae' (Romans 16:1), the noun diakonos. The Gospels name the women's service with the word Jesus chose for His own.
svg.text: THE SERVING WORD
διακονέω (diakoneō, G1247): to serve, to minister, to provide
Jesus, the One who serves
διακονῆσαι · ὡς ὁ διακονῶν
The Son of Man came not to be served but to
serve, and to give his life as a ransom for
many. … I am among you as the one who
serves.
Mark 10:45; Luke 22:27
The women of Galilee
διηκόνουν (Luke 8:3; Mark 15:41)
Mary, called Magdalene … and Joanna …
and Susanna, and many others, who
provided for them out of their means. …
they followed him and ministered to him.
Luke 8:2-3; Mark 15:41
Phoebe of Cenchreae
διάκονον · προστάτις
Our sister Phoebe, a servant of the
church at Cenchreae … she has been a
patron of many and of myself as well.
Romans 16:1-2
the same word
WHAT THE WORD SAYS
Luke names the women beside the Twelve: “the twelve were with him, and also some women”
(Luke 8:1-2). The verb is imperfect: they kept on providing. Mark adds that they followed
Him from Galilee and stood at the cross (Mark 15:40-41). Jesus chose the same verb for His
own mission (Mark 10:45). Phoebe carries the word into the church, and the only New
Testament προστάτις, “patron”, is hers (Romans 16:2).
“Whoever would be great among you must be your servant.”
Mark 10:43, ESV
After the manner of Clarence Larkin · the-way.lewy.au
